doc.title: Catherine Russell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 26, 2018

title: First 45s, Motown bass lines and radio and TV
summary: She recalls buying a Supremes 45, loving bass lines, and listening to radio and watching variety shows.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You and I are similar in age, and I was a buyer of 45 RPMs and I wondered if that was the medium that you would have —

Oh yeah. I remember the first 45 I ever bought, which was by the Supremes, and I think it was “Can’t Hurry Love.” And it cost forty-seven cents. And I was staying with my grandparents in Harlem, cause my mother was working so I used to stay with relatives. And there was a little record store down the street from them on 130th and Amsterdam, and that was my first 45 and I still have it.
All right. Do you recall zoning in on certain parts of the music, rather than the whole thing. Like the back-up vocals, the bass line?

Bass lines, which is why I love swing music so much, because the bass moves. It makes you, I like anything — I like to move you know. I like that, I liked Motown, because of those bass lines — those great James Jamerson bass lines. I used to wonder, when I used to watch, I used to watch a lot of variety shows growing up. I don’t know if you did the same. So I was hooked on, we’d — my mother had a radio in the kitchen so we’d listen to everything from Arthur Godfrey Hour to William B. Williams who was a DJ in New York who had, he would play what is now known as the Great American Songbook. But his program was called Make Believe Ballroom. And so we’d listen to those. And then you were able to see everybody on T.V. at night. So if you heard Frank Sinatra in the

morning, or Tony Bennett or Dean Martin, Ella Fitzgerald, then maybe they’d be on somebody’s program at night. So it was really exciting to me. Then of course we’d watch a lot of Ed Sullivan, you know, on Sunday nights. And I would wonder sometimes like now I know why, but I would wonder okay you saw the group but then there was all this arrangement happening. Where are the other people? Where are the strings at? I hear strings. I hear horns. You know? And all I’m seeing is four guys or whatever, singing, with nothing there. It’s like I used to think okay, where is the orchestra? Is it the house orchestra or are their other people? So this is what I used to wonder.
